response:
I recommend keeping the approval decisions separate and reusing the screens and notifications. Your clarification establishes a meaningful difference: access approval needs independent authorization and a separate decision owner. A shared interface does not justify merging those responsibilities.

That gives you a practical route to cheaper changes: update common screens and notifications once, while each department retains the rules and ownership its approvals require. The tradeoff is maintaining separate decision logic, but merging it would introduce exceptions into a supposedly uniform process. Actual savings remain unverified.

Reconsider a shared process only if it preserves those boundaries more simply than the existing reuse approach. Nothing supplied establishes that benefit.

## Architectural Invariants

| Condition and scope | Verification | Enforcement | Failure impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Every access approval requires independent authorization and a decision owner separate from purchase approvals. Applies to access decisions, including through shared screens. | Requirement established by your clarification; actual behavior unverified. | Existing safeguards not supplied. Confirm that current approval controls preserve this boundary when shared screens change. | Access could be approved without the required independent authority. |
| Purchase approvals remain reversible when shared components are used. | Required behavior supplied; actual reversal behavior unverified. | Existing safeguards not supplied. Preserve the current reversal mechanism and verify it after relevant shared changes. | A shared change could remove a required purchase capability. |
